extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of Darwin's life; historians of science; general readers interested in the circumstances of Darwin's appointment to the Beagle
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations surrounding appointment of a naturalist to the HMS Beagle as presented in Darwin's autobiography: practical qualifications, personal character, recommendations, family/professional objections, and expedition preparations. Focuses on what recommending persons (Henslow, Peacock) and Captain Fitz-Roy sought and what Darwin/family considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical natural-history qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Must be 'amply qualified for collecting, observing, and noting, anything worthy to be noted in Natural History.' (Henslow's description of Darwin's suitability.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Henslow explicitly states the candidate need not be a finished naturalist but should be competent in practical field skills: collecting specimens, making observations, and recording noteworthy natural-history information. Emphasis on useful, observable skills rather than finished scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not required to be a 'finished' naturalist
rubrics_metrics.description: The candidate is not expected to be a FINISHED naturalist; rather, practical aptitude and potential suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Henslow: 'I state this not in the supposition of your being a FINISHED naturalist, but as amply qualified...' — implies selection values potential and practical competence over completed credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Companionability and gentlemanly conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Captain Fitz-Roy 'wants a man more as a companion than a mere collector, and would not take any one...who was not recommended to him likewise as a GENTLEMAN.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal comportment, manners, and ability to serve as a congenial shipboard companion are explicit selection criteria; recommendation must vouch for the candidate's status as a 'gentleman' and companionable temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation by trusted patrons
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointment depends on strong recommendation from respected persons (Henslow, Peacock).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peacock and Henslow act as recommenders; Peacock conveys Admiralty/Beaufort approval. Formal/informal endorsement by senior scientific/administrative figures is decisive ('Peacock has sole appointment of Naturalist').

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on zeal and spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The expedition is presented as 'a finer chance for a man of zeal and spirit' — enthusiasm and energy are required qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond technical skills, personal drive, curiosity, and eagerness to make the most of the opportunity are valued; candidate should be willing to take initiative and exploit available research chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and mentoring qualities (modelled by Henslow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Desirable mentor/colleague attributes include 'transparent sincerity', 'absence of all self-consciousness', 'winning courtesy', and a way of encouraging young naturalists without discouraging them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Henslow is described as making young people feel at ease, receiving trivial observations with interest, and correcting mistakes kindly so as to encourage accuracy. These interpersonal qualities are presented as exemplary for scientific teachers and valued colleagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of teaching and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Lectures should be 'universally popular, and as clear as daylight'; practical excursions and accessible presentation matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective communication — clear lectures and organized field excursions — is highlighted as a mark of excellence in a naturalist/teacher and as beneficial to students and younger naturalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even temper and lack of petty feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal character is one 'never once saw his temper even ruffled' and without 'paltry feeling of vanity, envy, or jealousy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional stability and the absence of petty competitiveness are framed as important moral qualities in a scientific man and implicitly desirable in a shipboard colleague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principled determination and moral firmness
rubrics_metrics.description: Benevolence combined with 'a vigorous and determined will' and strong principle: 'When principle came into play, no power on earth could have turned him one hair's-breadth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alongside kindness, a naturalist should possess resolute will and moral firmness — the character to act on principle when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical expedition preparations and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring necessary instruments (e.g., clinometer, hammer); measure and prepare; but avoid overpacking—Henslow warns 'by no means to make up my mind till I have had long conversations with Captains Beaufort and Fitz-Roy' and that young travellers 'fall into [the mistake of] taking many things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical readiness (appropriate instruments, measurements, maps) is important, but experienced advisers (the captains, Henslow) should be consulted to avoid unnecessary baggage; concentrate on essentials for fieldwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/administrative conditions of the appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiralty will furnish an official appointment and accommodation but may not give a salary; Peacock has the appointment at his disposal and Admiralty/Beaufort approval is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates should be aware of administrative realities: official status may be provided without pay, accommodations depend on the vessel, and some logistical/fiscal uncertainties may exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family/professional suitability concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections considered by Darwin's father: voyage might be 'disreputable to my character as a Clergyman', 'unfit me to settle down as a Clergyman', 'a wild scheme', 'accommodations uncomfortable', and 'a useless undertaking' for his profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection/acceptance decisions were weighed against family expectations and future professional prospects (especially for a clerical career); such social/professional consequences were treated as legitimate criteria by family advisers.
